newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE-Russian election losers got consolation prizes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Russian election losers got consolation prizes.

text.p: One year after President Boris Yeltsin won his second term in the Kremlin, most of the major candidates he defeated cannot complain they did not get a consolation prize.
Some have been admitted to the cosy world of Moscow's political elite, others have the won the halo of political martyr, something which is highly esteemed in Russia.
Only the future will show which prize was better in Russia's uncertain political world.

Yeltsin's main election rival, Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, and maverick ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky, who came fifth in the first round, control opposition parties but are widely regarded as new members of the elite club.

Yeltsin, who vowed not to let the communists return to power during his re-election campaign, said after his victory that he was ready to work with all major political forces as long as they play the game. Zyuganov and Zhirinovsky certainly do.
They wage a war of words with Yeltsin. Their political groups, which dominate the State Duma lower house, reject some government bills.

But when it comes to voting on crucial programmes, such as the budget or new tax code, the communist and ultra-nationalist deputies have generally preferred under-the-carpet bargaining and, perhaps surprisingly, often emerged on the Kremlin's side when it mattered most.

"Russia's parliamentary opposition is gradually becoming civilised," the liberal Sevodnya newspaper said. "It wants to fight for power according to accepted rules. The last thing it wants is to destabilise the system or let newcomers create fresh turmoil."
EMERGENCE OF THE "RESPONSIBLE OPPOSITION"
Rejecting proposals to try to oust the government, Zyuganov said this month: "We are the responsible opposition."
A fall in popularity and growing discontent among more radical party colleagues are part of the price Zyuganov and, to a lesser extent, Zhirinovsky pay for their respectability.

"Zyuganov now fears Yeltsin less than he fears a mutiny in his own ranks. He knows very well that, if Yeltsin dissolves the Duma, his party rivals are quite likely to topple him and stake on a new, more radical leader," Sevodnya said.
"Zyuganov now has something to lose. He is a hostage of his status."
Opinion polls show that if the political trend continues, Zyuganov has little hope of becoming president.

The communists and their allies have done well in regional elections this year. But most of their successful candidates have moved into their new offices vowing cooperation with the Kremlin in a clear sign of the changes in the political system.
LIBERALS STILL PLAY HARD TO GET
Liberal Grigory Yavlinsky, whose bitter criticism of Yeltsin brought him more than five million votes in the presidential election, is different.
He continues to play hard to get and has rejected offers to join the so-called "party of power". But time is against him.
Opinion polls show 37-year-old First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, a possible heir to Yeltsin, has successfully replaced Yavlinsky as the young and attractive reformist.
"It's quite easy. Nemtsov is doing what Yavlinsky is talking about," one analyst close to the government said.
LEBED PLAYS ON POLITICAL MARTYR IMAGE
In contrast to Zyuganov or Zhirinovsky, ex-general Alexander Lebed has staked much on his image as a political martyr.
Lebed came third in the first round of the election and joined Yeltsin's team before the runoff vote, helping the president secure re-election.
As a reward, Yeltsin named Lebed as secretary of his policy-making Security Council and gave him strong powers to end the unpopular war in the breakaway region of Chechnya.

Lebed struck a controversial peace deal with the rebels. But his uncompromising manner and his overt desire for more power put him at odds with most of the Kremlin establishement and Yeltsin sacked him after four months.

"Lebed left in deep mortification and with an aura of an honest and plain polititian ousted by wicked intriguers -- the package that helped Yeltsin become a national leader in the late 1980s," said the analyst close to the government.

"The difference is that Yeltsin's package took up a disillusioned country which wanted changes more than stability," he added. "The situation is still tough. But Lebed faces a recovering country which does not want new turmoil at all."

Lebed, 47, is building up his own nationalist party as a powerbase for the next presidential election in 2000. He is seen as a potential leading candidate but his personal image of a plain-speaking man of honour is challenged by others.

General Lev Rokhlin, a respected officer and major pro-government parliamentary figure, has ventured on to Lebed's territory by launching a crusade against Yeltsin's military reform plans and demanding better conditions for the military.
